name: Multi-Region Disaster Recovery with Warm Standby
description: Design a multi-Region disaster recovery architecture on AWS using the warm standby strategy with live data replication, automated failover, and infrastructure as code.
user_problem: Design a multi-Region disaster recovery architecture on AWS with the following requirements: (1) A warm standby strategy with a recovery Region that maintains a minimum deployment capable of handling requests at reduced capacity, (2) Live data replication across Regions with near-zero RPO, (3) Automated failover using DNS-based routing, (4) Auto-scaling infrastructure in the recovery Region that can scale up to full production capacity during failover, (5) Cross-Region backup and restore capabilities for point-in-time recovery, (6) Infrastructure as code for consistent deployment across Regions, (7) Health checks, monitoring, and alerting for both Regions.

reference_architecture.full_text:
Disaster recovery (DR) is the process of preparing for and recovering from a disaster event. Any event that prevents a workload or system from fulfilling its business objectives in its primary location is classified as a disaster, including natural disasters like earthquakes or floods, technical failures such as power or network loss, and human actions such as inadvertent or unauthorized modifications. The warm standby DR strategy offers a good balance of benefits and cost between pilot light and multi-site active/active strategies. The key DR objectives are Recovery Time Objective (RTO), the maximum acceptable delay between interruption and restoration of service, and Recovery Point Objective (RPO), the maximum acceptable amount of time since the last data recovery point. Lower RTO and RPO cost more in terms of spend on resources and operational complexity, so these objectives must provide appropriate value for the workload.

Warm Standby Strategy Overview: The warm standby strategy is an active/passive DR approach where the workload operates from a single AWS Region (the active or primary Region) and all requests are handled from this Region. A second Region (the passive or recovery Region) maintains a scaled-down but functional deployment. Unlike the pilot light strategy where compute resources are shut off (zero instances deployed), warm standby deploys a functional stack at reduced capacity that can handle requests but cannot handle production-level traffic. This is typically implemented with one Amazon EC2 instance per application tier in the recovery Region, compared to a full production fleet in the primary Region. If the passive stack were deployed at full capacity, the strategy would be known as hot standby. Because warm standby deploys a functional stack, it is easier to test recovery readiness using synthetic transactions compared to pilot light. RTO for warm standby is lower than pilot light because the recovery Region can handle traffic at reduced levels immediately and then requires only scaling out the existing deployment, rather than first deploying infrastructure from scratch.

Data Replication Layer: Both strategies replicate data from the primary Region to data resources in the recovery Region. Amazon Aurora Global Database replicates data from the primary Aurora cluster in the active Region to a read-only Aurora cluster in the recovery Region with sub-second replication lag, typically under one second. This achieves near-zero RPO because the recovery Region data is almost always up to date with the primary. The read replica in the recovery Region can be promoted to a full read-write cluster during failover. In addition to replication, continuous backups are maintained in the recovery Region. Aurora DB cluster snapshots provide point-in-time recovery capability. This is critical because when human action type disasters occur (such as accidental deletion or data corruption), replication will replicate the bad data to the recovery Region. Backups are necessary to enable restoration to the last known good state. Amazon S3 with Cross-Region Replication (CRR) automatically replicates objects from the primary Region S3 buckets to corresponding buckets in the recovery Region. S3 CRR supports replicating encrypted objects, replication time control (RTC) for 99.99% of objects replicated within 15 minutes, and replication metrics for monitoring. S3 versioning is enabled on both source and destination buckets to protect against accidental overwrites and deletions. For NoSQL workloads, Amazon DynamoDB Global Tables provide multi-Region, fully replicated tables with sub-second replication, and any table in any Region can accept write operations.

Compute Layer: In each Region, an Elastic Load Balancer (ELB) distributes incoming traffic to Amazon EC2 instances. An Application Load Balancer (ALB) operates at the application layer (Layer 7), providing advanced request routing, SSL/TLS termination, and health checking of registered targets. EC2 instances run in an Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling group that automatically adjusts the number of running instances based on demand. In the active Region, the Auto Scaling group runs at full production capacity with a minimum, desired, and maximum instance count configured for production traffic. In the recovery Region, the Auto Scaling group's minimum and desired count are set to a reduced number (for example, one instance per tier for warm standby, or zero for pilot light). During failover, the Auto Scaling group in the recovery Region scales up automatically or via CloudFormation parameter updates to meet production-level traffic. Amazon Machine Images (AMIs) are built and copied across Regions to ensure consistent instance configuration, including the operating system, installed packages, and application code. AMI IDs are Region-specific, so cross-Region AMI copying ensures that the recovery Region can launch identical instances.

Infrastructure as Code: AWS CloudFormation or AWS Cloud Development Kit (AWS CDK) enables infrastructure as code (IaC) for consistent, repeatable deployment across both Regions. Using CloudFormation parameters and conditional logic, a single template can create both active stacks (primary Region) and passive stacks (recovery Region). The CloudFormation template uses an ActiveOrPassive parameter: when set to 'active,' the Auto Scaling group deploys the full desired capacity; when set to 'passive,' the desired capacity is set to zero (pilot light) or a minimal count (warm standby). During recovery, the stack in the recovery Region is updated by changing the parameter value to 'active' using the AWS CLI command: aws cloudformation update-stack --stack-name SampleWebApp --use-previous-template --parameters ParameterKey=ActiveOrPassive,ParameterValue=active. This automatically scales the Auto Scaling group to production capacity.

Networking Layer: Amazon VPC in each Region provides isolated network environments. Each VPC contains public subnets for load balancers and NAT Gateways, and private subnets for EC2 application instances and Aurora database instances. Security groups act as virtual firewalls controlling inbound and outbound traffic at the instance level. Network Access Control Lists (NACLs) provide an additional layer of subnet-level security. NAT Gateways in public subnets enable instances in private subnets to access the internet for updates and patches while remaining inaccessible from the internet. Inter-Region connectivity can use VPC Peering or AWS Transit Gateway for private communication between the active and recovery Region VPCs if needed.

DNS and Failover: Amazon Route 53 provides DNS-based routing with health checks to detect failures in the active Region and automatically failover traffic to the recovery Region. Route 53 failover routing policy automatically sends traffic to the recovery Region if the primary endpoint is unhealthy based on configured health checks. Health checks can monitor server liveness metrics, service API error rates and response latencies, service validation tests using Amazon CloudWatch Synthetics canaries, and workload key performance indicators (KPIs). For manually initiated failover, Amazon Route 53 Application Recovery Controller (ARC) provides Route 53 health checks that act as on/off switches controllable via the highly available data plane API. Using the AWS CLI or SDK, operators toggle these switches to redirect traffic from the primary to the recovery Region. Alternatively, AWS Global Accelerator can implement failover by onboarding customer traffic at the closest of over 200 edge locations and routing over the AWS network to healthy endpoints, providing lower latencies.

Detection and Automation: Amazon CloudWatch monitors both Regions and triggers alarms based on workload health metrics. CloudWatch alarms evaluate service API metrics such as error rates and response latencies. CloudWatch Synthetics canaries create scripts that call services and validate responses, providing deep insight into workload health. CloudWatch anomaly detection identifies unusual patterns such as unexpected drops in order rates. Amazon EventBridge provides event-driven serverless automation that can orchestrate recovery steps automatically when a disaster is detected, such as triggering Lambda functions that update CloudFormation stacks, promote Aurora read replicas, and update Route 53 routing.

Monitoring and Compliance: AWS CloudTrail provides continuous monitoring and audit logging of account activity across both Regions, recording all API calls for security analysis, resource change tracking, and compliance. CloudWatch dashboards provide unified operational visibility across both Regions, showing infrastructure health, replication lag, and failover readiness status. Amazon SNS sends notifications to operations teams when health checks fail, alarms trigger, or failover events occur.

The end-to-end recovery process is as follows: (1) Detect - CloudWatch alarms and Synthetics canaries detect that the primary Region workload is unhealthy based on API error rates, latency, or KPI anomalies. EventBridge triggers automated notification and optionally initiates recovery. (2) Restore - The passive stack in the recovery Region is scaled up by updating the CloudFormation stack parameter from passive to active, which increases the Auto Scaling group capacity to production levels. Aurora Global Database promotes the recovery Region read replica to a primary writer. (3) Failover - Route 53 failover routing redirects traffic to the recovery Region endpoint, either automatically via health checks or manually via Route 53 Application Recovery Controller. Once the new primary Region is handling all production traffic, the team can investigate and remediate the affected Region for eventual fallback.
